opus-5.5.text:
I think that objection mostly misreads where things are heading. Yes, today a lot of this still looks like code, because that's the substrate we're used to. But the interesting shift is that the programming language is increasingly just English. I've joked that the hottest new programming language is English, and I mean it fairly literally. When you describe what you want to an agent, you're programming it. You're specifying intent, constraints, what "done" looks like. That's the essence of programming; the syntax was always incidental.

So I don't think ordinary people will need to write Python. What they'll need is to think clearly about what they want and to notice when the result is wrong. That's a real skill, and not trivial, but it's much more widely distributed than knowing how to set up a build system or debug a segfault.

Where I'd push back on the optimists is that we're not fully there yet. These systems are still somewhat jagged. They can do something brilliant and then make a mistake no human would make. Right now you still benefit enormously from being able to look under the hood, read the diff, and understand roughly what happened. So for the next stretch, I picture something like an autonomy slider. You give the agent a small, well-scoped chunk, you verify it quickly, and you gradually hand over more as trust builds. The people with technical background will slide that further, faster.

But over time, a lot of the scaffolding that requires code literacy gets absorbed into the tools. The interfaces get better at showing you what the agent did in a way you can verify without reading code: visual diffs, previews, tests in plain language. That verification loop is really the crux. If a normal person can quickly check "is this what I wanted," they don't need to write the code. So I'd say the objection is true for today's tooling, but it's describing a temporary state, not a fundamental barrier.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that ordinary people will not need to write code eventually, but gives no one-to-three-year timeframe.

r002.rationale: It describes users stating intent, constraints, and completion criteria in English so an agent can carry out the requested task, framing this as programming without code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that objection gets the direction of travel backwards. The whole point of what's happening is that the barrier to instructing a computer is collapsing. For most of computing history, if you wanted the machine to do something custom, you had to learn its language. Now the machine is learning yours. I've been calling this "vibe coding" half-jokingly, but the serious version of it is that English is becoming the programming language, and the model is the compiler.

So when people say "ordinary people can't write code," I'd say, well, they already don't, and they're still getting things done. If you watch someone who has never programmed sit down with one of these agents, they describe what they want, they look at the result, they say "no, not like that, more like this," and they iterate. That loop of specify, inspect, correct is exactly what programmers do. The syntax was never the hard part. The hard part is knowing what you want and being able to tell whether you got it, and that's a very human skill that lots of non-programmers have.

Now, I do want to be fair to the objection, because there is a real version of it. Writing code was never just typing. It was a way of forcing yourself to be precise about the problem. When you remove that forcing function, people can end up with something that looks like it works and doesn't, and they don't have the mental model to notice. I've felt this myself even as someone who does know how to code. You get a lot of output, it runs, and you're not quite sure it's correct. So there's a verification gap, and I think the tooling has to close it. Better ways to see what the agent did, to test it, to roll back. The agent has to earn trust incrementally rather than dumping ten thousand lines on you.

The other thing I'd say is that it's a spectrum, not a binary. A lot of people are going to be in the middle, where they're not writing code from scratch but they do develop some intuition for how software is structured, because they're reading what the agent produced and nudging it. I think that's actually a great outcome. Computer literacy goes up, not down. More people understand what a program is, what a loop is, what a bug looks like, because they encounter those things constantly through the agent rather than through a textbook.

So my overall take is that the automation doesn't require ordinary people to write code. It requires them to be able to think clearly about what they want and to check the work. And honestly, that's the part I'd want them to focus on anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says the automation does not require ordinary people to write code, but gives no prediction or timeframe of roughly one to three years.

r002.rationale: It presents understanding natural-language instructions and turning them into results as central to the agent: nonprogrammers describe what they want, inspect the result, and iterate.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think ordinary people should have to write code. The whole point is that you can express what you want in natural language, and the agent handles the implementation. Code may still be the thing that runs underneath, but it doesn’t have to be the interface you interact with.

Now, that doesn’t mean there’s no work for the person. You still have to explain what you want, give the system enough context, and check whether it actually did the right thing. And sometimes describing what you want precisely is surprisingly hard. So I think the skill shifts from writing every instruction yourself to specifying the goal and supervising the result.

Knowing how to program gives you a lot of additional control. You can look under the hood when something goes wrong. But that should be an advantage, rather than a prerequisite for getting useful work out of these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary people should not have to write code, but gives no prediction or one-to-three-year timeframe.

r002.rationale: It presents expressing a goal in natural language and having the agent implement it as “the whole point,” characterizing that translation as a central capability for ordinary users.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think it requires ordinary people to write code. It requires them to express what they want, and then the agent can write the code. That’s a pretty significant change in who can program a computer. You can describe a task in English, give examples, and iterate on the result.

But there’s still a question of how much you can delegate reliably. If the agent builds something, can you tell whether it works? Can you recognize when it’s done the wrong thing? So I think the bottleneck moves from writing the implementation to specifying the intent and evaluating the outcome. Knowing how to code still helps enormously, because you can inspect what’s happening and intervene. But it doesn’t have to be the entry requirement.

r001.rationale: The response says code need not be an entry requirement, but gives no prediction or one-to-three-year timeframe.

r002.rationale: It says users can describe a task in English and the agent can write the code, framing intent translation as the way to use the agent.
